about: The open weights for the five parcel pillars. Every indicator, source, normalization rule, weight and gate lives here; the build script, the scorer, the methodology page and the chatbot all read this file. Change a weight here (or pass an override file to score-parcels.ts) and every score changes. Weights are value judgments, not data.
scale: Every indicator, sub-score and pillar is 0–100, where 100 means this is a good place to build new housing and 0 means a poor one.
reference: Area indicators are percentile-ranked across all Allegheny County units in their source file (block groups, tracts or ZIPs); parcel indicators use fixed thresholds.

missing.rule: exclude and renormalize the remaining weights

overall.rationale: Weighted geometric mean limits how much a strong pillar can offset a weak one (UN HDI, 2010 switch; OECD/JRC Handbook 2008). Scores are floored at 1 so a zero doesn't zero the product. Arithmetic is available as a toggle.

pillars.label: Demand
pillars.description: Is there demand for new homes here? Household and job growth, low vacancy, an active sales market, rising rents and recent construction score high.

pillars.label: Site Feasibility
pillars.description: Can this lot physically take new housing? Flooding, steep slopes, landslides, undermining and known lead service lines score low. Zoning legality is applied per housing type, not averaged in.

gates.flag: Part of the lot is in the FEMA regulatory floodway

pillars.label: Housing Need & Displacement Risk
pillars.description: Two sub-scores. Housing need: where renters are most cost-burdened, new homes are needed most, so high burden scores high. Displacement risk: where prices and rents are surging, new building can speed displacement, so high pressure scores low.

subscores.label: Housing need
subscores.description: Unmet need for homes people can afford: cost burden, rent relative to area median income, housing + transportation and energy costs. 100 = greatest need.

subscores.label: Displacement risk
subscores.description: Signs that rising costs are pushing residents out: fast rent and price growth, sale prices outpacing incomes. 100 = low risk.

pillars.direction_note: Value judgment: need raises the score (the CDC and planner view of 'a good place to build'), displacement pressure lowers it. A market-first view would score high rents as good; the market_first preset leans that way.

pillars.label: Access to Opportunity
pillars.description: Would new residents reach daily needs? Walking distance to groceries, health care, schools and services, transit service, and jobs reachable by transit.

pillars.label: Climate & Environment
pillars.description: Would homes here be low-carbon and healthy? Two sub-scores that often pull in opposite directions: carbon (dense, walkable places mean less driving) and local environment (air, heat, tree canopy). Kept separate so the trade-off stays visible.

subscores.label: Carbon (location efficiency)
subscores.description: Transportation emissions a household here would likely produce. Building-form carbon depends on the housing type and is added when types are compared.

subscores.label: Local environment
subscores.description: Air pollution, industrial emissions, surface heat and tree canopy where residents would live.

indicators.label: Household change, 2020 Census to ACS 2020–24
indicators.rationale: Household growth is the core of HUD market-analysis demand. Weak signal: only 35 of 394 tracts change by more than the ACS margin of error, so it carries weight 1.

indicators.label: Home sales per 100 housing units, 2024–25
indicators.rationale: Arm's-length residential sales (county sales file) relative to housing stock: an active market absorbs new homes.

indicators.label: Residential vacancy (USPS)
indicators.rationale: Low vacancy means existing homes are being absorbed.

indicators.label: Job change, 2019 to 2023
indicators.rationale: Employment growth drives household formation (LEHD LODES).

indicators.label: Rent growth, last 12 months (Zillow ZORI)
indicators.rationale: Rising asking rents signal demand exceeding supply.

indicators.label: New residential permits within 800 m
indicators.rationale: Revealed demand: builders are already building nearby. City of Pittsburgh permits only.

indicators.label: Market Value Analysis type (A strongest … J most distressed)
indicators.rationale: Default weight 0: rewarding strong markets steers housing away from distressed neighborhoods. Available for users who choose to weigh it.

indicators.label: Share of lot in the FEMA regulatory floodway
indicators.rationale: Used only as a gate (caps the pillar at 20); never averaged.

indicators.label: Share of lot in the 100-year floodplain
indicators.rationale: FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area; triggers the City floodplain overlay (Ch. 906).

indicators.label: Share of lot at 25%+ slope (City map, 2018)
indicators.rationale: Triggers the City steep-slope overlay (Ch. 906) and raises foundation cost.

indicators.label: Share of lot in a City landslide-prone area
indicators.rationale: Triggers the City landslide-prone overlay (Ch. 906).

indicators.label: Share of lot on a mapped recent landslide deposit (county)
indicators.rationale: County susceptibility mapping; complements the City overlay.

indicators.label: Share of lot over mapped mines (City undermined area)
indicators.rationale: Triggers the City undermined overlay (Ch. 906); subsidence risk.

indicators.label: Known lead or galvanized service line at this address
indicators.rationale: Replacement adds cost. Unknown or unmatched addresses are missing, not 'no lead'.

indicators.label: FEMA NRI inland flooding score
indicators.rationale: Uses the NRI hazard score, not expected annual loss, which scales with property value.

indicators.label: Easiest legal pathway for mainstream housing types (current code)
indicators.rationale: Not averaged into Site Feasibility. It multiplies the overall score instead (see the legal block in this file).

indicators.label: Low-income renters paying 30%+ of income on housing (CHAS)
indicators.rationale: HUD's 30% cost-burden standard for households at or below 80% AMI. More burdened renters = more need for homes they can afford.

indicators.label: Median gross rent vs. rent affordable at 50% AMI (3-person household)
indicators.rationale: 1242.5 = 30% × $49,700 (HUD FY2026 Pittsburgh 50% AMI, 3 persons) ÷ 12. Rent at 2× what a 50% AMI household can afford scores 100 (high need); 0.8× or less scores 0. The household size is an assumption.

indicators.label: Renters paying 30%+ of income on rent (ACS)
indicators.rationale: All renters, not just low-income; ACS margins of error are large at block group level.

indicators.label: Housing + transportation cost share, median-income family (HUD LAI v3)
indicators.rationale: CNT's H+T benchmark treats ≤45% of income as affordable, so 45% scores 0 need and 75% scores 100. The 75% point is our assumption. Modeled for a fixed household; inputs 2012–16 on 2010 tracts.

indicators.label: Rent growth, last 5 years (Zillow ZORI)
indicators.rationale: Fast rent growth is a displacement pressure (Urban Displacement Project typology uses rent change).

indicators.label: Displacement Risk Ratio, 2019/20 (Reinvestment Fund)
indicators.rationale: Sale-price growth relative to residents' incomes (Reinvestment Fund). Data end 2019/20, so low weight; tract price growth carries the current signal.

indicators.label: Median home sale price change, 2020–21 to 2024–25
indicators.rationale: Fast price appreciation is the market-pressure signal in the Urban Displacement Project and Portland (Bates 2013) methods. Pooled two-year medians; tracts with fewer than 10 sales in a pool are blank.

indicators.label: Eviction filings per 100 renter households, 2025
indicators.rationale: Context only (weight 0): Eviction Lab publishes only ZIP-level filings for Allegheny County, and the ZIP value barely relates to the other displacement signals (r = −0.05).

indicators.label: Home energy burden, households at or below 80% AMI (DOE LEAD 2022)
indicators.rationale: Energy bills are part of housing cost. Modeled from ACS 2022 PUMS, not utility bills.

indicators.label: Weekday transit trips within 800 m, distance-weighted
indicators.rationale: Transit Score pattern: trips × mode weight × distance decay.

indicators.label: Walking distance to nearest grocery
indicators.rationale: Full-service groceries from USDA SNAP retailers + ACHD food permits (deduped, tier full_grocery). Walk Score decay: full credit within 400 m, none beyond 2.4 km. Straight-line distance.

indicators.label: Walking distance to nearest pharmacy
indicators.rationale: Retail pharmacies from the CMS NPPES registry (2026), with closed Rite Aid stores removed.

indicators.label: Walking distance to nearest school
indicators.rationale: Proximity only; school quality is deliberately not scored.

indicators.label: Walking distance to nearest park
indicators.rationale: Distance to the nearest park boundary vertex.

indicators.label: Distance to nearest health center, clinic or hospital
indicators.rationale: HRSA health-center sites, NPPES urgent-care/primary-care/community clinics, and hospitals.

indicators.label: Walking distance to nearest child care
Walking distance to nearest library
Walking distance to nearest food pantry or walk-up food distribution
indicators.rationale: Greater Pittsburgh Community Food Bank network (Apr 2025). Drive-up distributions are excluded because they are scheduled events, not places you can walk to.

indicators.label: Distance to nearest dentist
indicators.rationale: OSM + County Assets. No data on which dentists accept Medicaid.

indicators.label: Walking distance to nearest community center
Distance to nearest senior center
indicators.rationale: Matters most for older adults; the older-adult preset raises Access overall.

indicators.label: Jobs reachable within 30 minutes by transit
indicators.rationale: Cumulative-opportunity accessibility (EPA Smart Location Database style).

indicators.label: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5), PA percentile
indicators.rationale: EJScreen v2.3 modeled annual exposure, re-ranked within the county.

indicators.label: Traffic combustion (mean of diesel PM, NO2 and traffic proximity percentiles)
indicators.rationale: Three correlated traffic indicators averaged first so traffic counts once.

indicators.label: Industrial air toxics (RSEI), PA percentile
Industrial criteria-pollutant emissions nearby, distance-weighted (ACHD, ≤2021)
indicators.rationale: Tons/yr from current permitted facilities, full weight within 1 km, fading to zero at 5 km. Emissions, not measured exposure; NRG Cheswick may have retired after 2021.

indicators.label: Modeled annual household VMT, median-income family (HUD LAI v3)
indicators.rationale: Transportation-carbon proxy. HUD models VMT for a fixed household (median income, 4 people, 2 commuters), so it varies only with location efficiency. Inputs 2012–16, 2010 tracts.

indicators.label: FEMA NRI heat wave score
indicators.rationale: FEMA NRI heat wave score. Little variation within the county, so low weight; surface temperature carries most of the heat signal.

indicators.label: Summer surface heat, parcel (Landsat 8, 4-scene anomaly vs county median)
indicators.rationale: Mean of (LST − scene county median) over 4 clear summer scenes, 2023–2025. Surface, not air, temperature; ranked, not thresholded.

indicators.label: Tree canopy at the parcel (NLCD 2021, 30 m)
indicators.rationale: Canopy cools and filters air. 50%+ canopy scores 100. The 30 m grid misses small street trees.

sensitivity.rationale: Dirichlet draws around the current pillar weights. Concentration 47 gives a 0.2 weight a standard deviation of about 0.058, matching the ±0.1 uniform weight ranges used in the JRC audit of the Global Innovation Index.

units.fraction_pct: value is a fraction; shown ×100 as %

legal.description: Whether current zoning lets you build the brief's mainstream housing types (detached, townhouse, two-unit, three-unit, multi-unit) on this parcel. The overall score is multiplied by the factor for the easiest legal pathway among them. Legality is read from the City use table (§911.02), not estimated.

levels.label: Housing allowed with Zoning Administrator approval
Housing needs a ZBA special exception
levels.note: ZBA approved 90% of special exceptions in 2023–26 (n=30), counting only posted decisions.

levels.label: Housing needs conditional use (Planning Commission + Council)
Housing not permitted, but the parcel borders a district that allows it
levels.note: Exceptions happen at district edges: a use variance (73% approved, n=30) or a map amendment extending the neighboring district (Council adopted all 42 rezonings since 2015). Still a long, uncertain process.

levels.label: Housing not permitted: needs a rezoning or use variance
levels.note: Not legally impossible, but the slowest, least certain path.

levels.label: Planned district: depends on the site's approved plan
Outside City zoning jurisdiction (Mount Oliver Borough)

legal.rationale: The multipliers are value judgments about how much approval risk should cost. 'Not permitted' is penalized heavily (×0.2) but not zeroed, because rezonings and use variances do get approved, especially where a parcel borders a district that already allows housing (×0.5).

overall.text: A strong place to build new housing.
A good place to build, with some trade-offs.
A mixed case: real strengths and real drawbacks.
A hard place to build new housing right now.

demand.text: People really want to live here: households, sales and construction are active.
Not many people are looking to move here right now.

site.text: An easy lot to build on: no major physical hazards.
Mostly buildable, with minor site constraints.
Real site constraints (slope, landslide, undermining or flood) to work around.
Hard to build here: serious physical hazards.

afford.text: High need for homes people can afford, with little displacement risk.
Clear need for affordable homes and manageable displacement risk.
Need and displacement risk pull against each other here.
Either housing is already fairly affordable or displacement risk is high.

affordability.text: Housing costs are a real burden here: new affordable homes are badly needed.
Many renters are stretched: clear need for affordable homes.
Fairly affordable already: less need for new affordable homes.

displacement.text: Prices are stable: little displacement pressure.
Prices are rising: watch for displacement.
Prices are surging: new building here risks pushing people out.

access.text: Everything is close: transit, groceries, health care and services.
Some needs are walkable; others take a car or bus.
Car-dependent: daily needs are far away.

climate.text: A low-carbon, healthy place to live.
Mostly good on carbon and environment.
Trade-offs between low driving and local air, heat or tree cover.
High driving emissions and a poor local environment.

carbon.text: Residents here would drive very little.

local_env.text: Clean air, cooler surfaces and good tree cover.
Some air pollution, heat or missing tree cover.
Poor air quality and hot, paved surroundings.
